duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.t: The Dutch half of Limburg, made a duchy of the German Confederation in 1839 to compensate the Confederation for losing part of Luxembourg.
duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.o: The Treaty of London of 1839 divided Limburg between Belgium and the Netherlands. Because the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg lost its western half to Belgium, the Dutch part of Limburg was made a duchy and joined the German Confederation, held by the Dutch king, though Maastricht and Venlo were left outside the Confederation.
duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.r: The duchy was governed as a Dutch province while its estates sent representatives to the Confederation's diet in Frankfurt. In 1848 some Limburgers sought separation from the Netherlands to join Germany, and deputies sat in the Frankfurt Parliament. Mining and Maastricht's pottery and glass industries developed.
duchy-of-limburg-1839-1867.e: The German Confederation dissolved after the war of 1866, and the Treaty of London of 1867 confirmed that Limburg was fully part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The title 'Duchy of Limburg' lingered in official use until 1906.

duchy-of-aquitaine.t: The great duchy of south-western France, home of troubadour courts and Eleanor of Aquitaine, fought over by the kings of England and France for three centuries.
duchy-of-aquitaine.o: The Frankish kingdom of Aquitaine dissolved in the late 9th century, and in 893 William the Pious, count of Auvergne, took the ducal title; he founded the abbey of Cluny in 910. From the mid-10th century the counts of Poitou, the Ramnulfids, held the duchy and ruled from Poitiers.
duchy-of-aquitaine.r: The dukes ruled loosely over powerful vassals in Gascony, the Limousin and Auvergne. Their court was a centre of Occitan culture: Duke William IX is the earliest known troubadour. Bordeaux grew rich on wine exports to England. Eleanor of Aquitaine brought the duchy first to Louis VII of France and then, in 1152, to Henry II, joining it to the Angevin Empire.
duchy-of-aquitaine.e: English kings held the duchy as vassals of France, reduced after 1204 to Gascony, or Guyenne, and confirmed by the Treaty of Paris of 1259. Disputes over it helped spark the Hundred Years' War, which ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 and the annexation of Guyenne to the Kingdom of France.

duchy-of-castro.t: A Farnese duchy in northern Lazio created by Pope Paul III for his son, whose capital was razed by a later pope in 1649.
duchy-of-castro.o: In 1537 Pope Paul III, born Alessandro Farnese, carved the Duchy of Castro out of the Papal States for his son Pier Luigi Farnese. It covered the old Farnese estates between Lake Bolsena and the Tyrrhenian coast.
duchy-of-castro.r: Castro was rebuilt as a small Renaissance capital, with buildings by Antonio da Sangallo the Younger. After 1545 its dukes were also dukes of the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza, and they ran Castro from afar, borrowing heavily against it. A quarrel over these debts and the Farnese's power led Pope Urban VIII to fight the First War of Castro in 1641–1644, which ended in a papal setback.
duchy-of-castro.e: In 1649, after the murder of the new bishop of Castro was blamed on the Farnese, Pope Innocent X's troops took the town and razed it to the ground. The duchy was absorbed into the Papal States.

duchy-of-westphalia.t: Ducal territory in the Sauerland held for six centuries by the archbishops of Cologne after the fall of Henry the Lion.
duchy-of-westphalia.o: When Henry the Lion was deposed, the Gelnhausen Charter of 1180 split his Duchy of Saxony. The western part, with the title Duke of Westphalia and Engern, went to Archbishop Philip of Heinsberg of Cologne. The archbishops turned this title into real rule over the Sauerland, buying the County of Arnsberg in 1368.
duchy-of-westphalia.r: Ruled by the Electorate of Cologne as a separate territory, the duchy had its own estates and diet meeting at Arnsberg, with an electoral governor there. The land was hilly and rural, known for iron working and forestry. Cologne's ambitions in the region were checked by its defeat at Worringen in 1288 and by the Soest Feud, in which Soest broke away to Cleves. The duchy stayed Catholic throughout.
duchy-of-westphalia.e: In 1803 the duchy was secularised and given to Hesse-Darmstadt. The Congress of Vienna transferred it to Prussia in 1816, and it became part of the Prussian Province of Westphalia; it now lies in North Rhine-Westphalia.

duchy-of-lotharingia.t: The duchy that held together the old middle kingdom of Lothair II, between France and Germany, before it was split into Upper and Lower Lorraine in 959.
duchy-of-lotharingia.o: Lotharingia was the kingdom created for Lothair II in 855, stretching from Frisia to the Vosges. After the Carolingian lines weakened, the East Frankish king Louis the Child appointed Gebhard as duke in 903. Local nobles, led by the Reginarids, repeatedly switched allegiance between East and West Francia.
duchy-of-lotharingia.r: The duchy held the old Carolingian heartland around Aachen, Trier, Metz and Liège, rich in bishoprics and royal abbeys. Duke Gilbert went over to the West Frankish king before Henry the Fowler recovered the region in 925; Gilbert drowned at Andernach in 939 while rebelling against Otto I. Otto's son-in-law Conrad the Red rebelled in 953.
duchy-of-lotharingia.e: Otto I then gave the duchy to his brother Bruno, archbishop of Cologne, who divided it in 959 into the Duchy of Upper Lorraine and the Duchy of Lower Lorraine. Upper Lorraine became the later Duchy of Lorraine; the Low Countries principalities grew out of Lower Lorraine.
duchy-of-lotharingia.la: Old French and Old High German

duchy-of-lower-lorraine.t: The northern half of old Lotharingia, a duchy over the Low Countries whose title was carried by Godfrey of Bouillon and survived in Brabant.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.o: In 959 Archbishop Bruno of Cologne divided the Duchy of Lotharingia, creating a separate duchy for the lands of the lower Meuse, Scheldt and Rhine. The German kings appointed its dukes, including the Carolingian Charles, brother of the West Frankish king Lothair, from 977 to 991.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.r: Ducal power was always limited, since counts such as those of Louvain, Hainaut, Namur, Holland and Limburg and the prince-bishops of Liège and Utrecht built their own principalities. The emperors used the office to reward loyal families: Godfrey the Bearded's house held it, and Godfrey of Bouillon was duke before leading the First Crusade in 1096.
duchy-of-lower-lorraine.e: From 1106 the title was disputed between the counts of Louvain and Limburg. At the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in 1190 Emperor Henry VI limited the duke's authority to his own lands, and the Louvain dukes thereafter ruled as dukes of Brabant, keeping the title duke of Lothier.

duchy-of-styria.t: Alpine duchy of Graz and the Erzberg iron mountain, a Habsburg land for over six centuries and the shield of Inner Austria against the Ottomans.
duchy-of-styria.o: The March of Styria grew from a Carolingian border zone ruled from the 11th century by the Otakar counts of Steyr. In 1180 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised it to a duchy for Ottokar IV. By the Georgenberg Pact of 1186 it passed to the Babenbergs of the Duchy of Austria in 1192, and after Ottokar II of Bohemia it came to the Habsburgs in 1282.
duchy-of-styria.r: Styria was governed by its dukes with strong estates meeting in the Landhaus at Graz. Iron from the Erzberg made it an industrial heartland. From 1564 Graz was capital of Inner Austria under Archduke Charles II, who invited the Jesuits; his son Ferdinand II expelled Protestants. Repeated Ottoman raids made defence a constant concern. German was spoken in the north and Slovene in Lower Styria.
duchy-of-styria.e: Styria remained a crown land of the Habsburg Monarchy and Austria-Hungary until 1918. It was then divided: Lower Styria with Maribor went to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and is now in Slovenia, while the rest became the Austrian state of Styria.

duchy-of-the-archipelago.t: Latin duchy of the Cyclades centred on Naxos, founded by the Venetian Marco Sanudo, which outlived most crusader states in Greece by more than a century.
duchy-of-the-archipelago.o: Around 1207 Marco Sanudo, nephew of the doge Enrico Dandolo, led a private Venetian expedition that conquered Naxos and other Cycladic islands, sharing some with fellow adventurers. He took the title Duke of the Archipelago under the suzerainty of the Latin Empire and later of the Principality of Achaea.
duchy-of-the-archipelago.r: The dukes ruled from the Kastro of Naxos, granting fiefs to Latin lords on islands such as Andros, Paros and Milos. A Catholic minority lived alongside a Greek Orthodox majority, which kept its church. Revenues came from agriculture, emery and trade. In 1383 Francesco I Crispo seized the duchy and founded a new dynasty.
duchy-of-the-archipelago.e: Barbarossa's raids of 1537 made the duchy an Ottoman tributary. In 1566 the Ottomans deposed Giacomo IV Crispo and gave the duchy to the Jewish financier Joseph Nasi, who ruled through a deputy. After his death in 1579 it was annexed to the Ottoman Empire.

duchy-of-normandy.t: The Viking settlement on the lower Seine that became one of Europe's best-run principalities and launched the Norman conquest of England.
duchy-of-normandy.o: In 911, by the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, King Charles the Simple granted lands around Rouen to the Viking leader Rollo in return for defending the Seine. Rollo's descendants expanded westwards to the Cotentin, adopted Christianity and the French language, and were styled dukes by the early 11th century.
duchy-of-normandy.r: The dukes built unusually firm control over their barons, castles and the Church. Monasteries such as Jumièges, Fécamp, Bec and Mont-Saint-Michel flourished, and Bec produced the scholars Lanfranc and Anselm. Normans also carved out lands in southern Italy and Sicily. In 1066 Duke William won the battle of Hastings and became king of England.
duchy-of-normandy.e: Normandy passed to the Plantagenets and formed a pillar of the Angevin Empire. Philip II of France took Château Gaillard and Rouen in 1204, annexing the duchy to the Kingdom of France. The Channel Islands remained with the English crown.

duchy-of-thuringia.t: A Frankish frontier duchy in central Germany, set up against the Slavs, whose dukes briefly ruled almost independently before Carolingian absorption.
duchy-of-thuringia.o: After the Franks destroyed the Kingdom of the Thuringians in 531, the area was ruled by Frankish officials. Around 631 King Dagobert I appointed Radulf duke to defend the eastern frontier against the Slavs of Samo's Empire, then raiding Thuringia. Radulf soon defeated Dagobert's son Sigebert III in 641 and ruled as a near-independent king.
duchy-of-thuringia.r: Later Thuringia was held by the Hedenid dukes, based at Würzburg on the Main. Duke Heden II supported the Anglo-Saxon missionary Willibrord, who received estates at Arnstadt in 704, and a church was founded on the Marienberg at Würzburg. The duchy guarded the border with the Saxons and the Sorbs.
duchy-of-thuringia.e: Heden II disappears around 717 to 719, perhaps after the Battle of Vincy, and Charles Martel brought Thuringia under direct Frankish control. Saint Boniface reorganised its church, founding the bishopric of Würzburg in 742. The region later formed part of the Duchy of Saxony and the Landgraviate of Thuringia.

daorsi.t: Hellenised Illyrian people of the lower Neretva, whose walled hill town of Daorson near Stolac minted its own coins.
daorsi.o: The Daorsi emerged in the Neretva valley of Herzegovina, in contact with Greek traders at Narona and the island colonies of the Adriatic. By the 3rd century BCE they had a fortified centre at Daorson, on a hill near modern Stolac, enclosed by massive Cyclopean walls.
daorsi.r: Greek influence was strong: the Daorsi struck bronze coins with Greek legends, used Greek-style buildings and traded wine, oil and pottery through the Neretva. They broke with the Illyrian king Gentius and sided with Rome in 168 BCE, which rewarded them with exemption from tribute. Their wealthier neighbours, the Delmatae, repeatedly attacked them.
daorsi.e: Daorson was destroyed in the mid-1st century BCE, probably by the Delmatae. The Daorsi were absorbed into Roman Illyricum by the end of the 1st century BCE, and their region later belonged to the province of Dalmatia.

ditadura-nacional.t: The military dictatorship that ended Portugal's First Republic and brought António de Oliveira Salazar to power.
ditadura-nacional.o: On 28 May 1926 a military coup launched from Braga by General Manuel Gomes da Costa overthrew the First Portuguese Republic. Within weeks Gomes da Costa was pushed aside by General Óscar Carmona, who became president.
ditadura-nacional.r: The military regime dissolved parliament, introduced censorship and repressed several revolts. Unable to solve the financial crisis, it appointed the Coimbra economics professor António de Oliveira Salazar as finance minister in 1928, with control over all spending. He balanced the budget and steadily accumulated power, becoming prime minister in 1932.
ditadura-nacional.e: A new constitution, approved by plebiscite in 1933, transformed the military dictatorship into Salazar's civilian, corporatist Estado Novo (Portugal), with Carmona remaining president.

duchy-of-montferrat.t: A Piedmontese duchy of the Gonzaga, whose fortress of Casale was one of the most contested strongholds in 17th-century Europe.
duchy-of-montferrat.o: The Gonzaga of the Duchy of Mantua had inherited the March of Montferrat in 1536. In 1574 Emperor Maximilian II raised it to a duchy for Duke Guglielmo Gonzaga, who governed it from Mantua through a council at Casale.
duchy-of-montferrat.r: Montferrat was a hilly wine-growing region split into two parts and surrounded by the Duchy of Savoy and the Duchy of Milan. Its local nobles resented Mantuan rule. Vincenzo I Gonzaga built the great citadel of Casale around 1590. When the main Gonzaga line died out in 1627, the War of the Mantuan Succession brought sieges of Casale by Spain and Savoy against France. The Peace of Cherasco in 1631 gave parts to Savoy and the rest to Charles I Gonzaga-Nevers.
duchy-of-montferrat.e: The last duke, Ferdinando Carlo, sided with France and was deposed in 1708. Montferrat was given to the Duchy of Savoy, a transfer confirmed by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713.

durotriges.t: Dorset confederation of hillfort dwellers whose resistance ended when Vespasian's legion stormed strongholds such as Maiden Castle and Hod Hill.
durotriges.o: The Durotriges took shape in the late Iron Age across Dorset and neighbouring parts of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, a landscape dominated by great multivallate hillforts. Their harbour at Hengistbury Head traded with Armorica in the 1st century BCE, bringing in Italian wine amphorae and Gaulish pottery in exchange for metals, grain and cattle.
durotriges.r: Power seems to have been spread among several centres rather than held by one king, and no ruler's name appears on their coins, which became crude cast and debased silver issues. Hillforts such as Maiden Castle were heavily refortified and stocked with sling stones. The Durotriges buried their dead in crouched inhumations, unlike the cremation rites of the south-east, and Kimmeridge shale was worked into bracelets.
durotriges.e: In 43 and 44 the future emperor Vespasian, leading the legio II Augusta, took more than twenty strongholds in the south-west according to Suetonius; a Roman fort was built inside Hod Hill. The territory became the civitas of the Durotriges with its centre at Durnovaria, modern Dorchester, within Roman Britain.

duchy-of-guastalla.t: A small Po valley state first ruled by the Torelli and then by a branch of the Gonzaga, before joining Parma in 1748.
duchy-of-guastalla.o: In 1406 Guido Torelli, a condottiere in the service of the Visconti, received Guastalla, a town on the Po between Mantua and Parma. The Torelli ruled it as counts under the overlordship of the Duchy of Milan.
duchy-of-guastalla.r: In 1539 Countess Ludovica Torelli sold Guastalla to Ferrante Gonzaga, general of Charles V and governor of Milan, whose branch of the Gonzaga ruled it from then on. Ferrante II was made duke in 1621. The duchy was a fortified town with its farmland, and its rulers were often drawn into the quarrels over the Duchy of Mantua.
duchy-of-guastalla.e: The Guastalla Gonzaga died out in 1746. By the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 the duchy was given to Philip of Bourbon and joined to the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza.

duchy-of-saint-sava.t: Domain of the Kosača family whose ruler's title, herceg, gave the region of Herzegovina its name.
duchy-of-saint-sava.o: Stjepan Vukčić Kosača inherited the lands of Hum and the coast from his uncle Sandalj Hranić in 1435, becoming the mightiest noble of the Kingdom of Bosnia. In 1448 he styled himself Herceg of Saint Sava, after the relics of the Serbian saint kept at the monastery of Mileševa in his territory, asserting independence from the Bosnian king.
duchy-of-saint-sava.r: From his castle at Blagaj near Mostar, Stjepan controlled the caravan routes between the Adriatic and the interior, levying customs on trade with Ragusa and founding the port of Novi, today Herceg Novi. His lands mixed adherents of the Bosnian Church, Orthodox and Catholic Christians, and he quarrelled with Ragusa, Venice and his own son Vladislav.
duchy-of-saint-sava.e: The Ottomans conquered Bosnia in 1463 and most of Stjepan's lands by 1465; he died in 1466. His son Vlatko held a shrinking coastal remnant until Herceg Novi fell in 1482. Another son converted and became the Ottoman grand vizier Hersekzade Ahmed Pasha.

dobunni.t: Cotswold kingdom whose coins name a string of rulers, and whose Roman town at Cirencester became the second largest in Britain.
dobunni.o: The Dobunni held Gloucestershire, north Somerset, Worcestershire and parts of Oxfordshire and Wiltshire in the late Iron Age. By the 1st century BCE they were minting coins, and a large oppidum developed at Bagendon near Cirencester, with Roman imports reaching it before the conquest.
dobunni.r: Their gold and silver coins carry the names of rulers such as Corio, Bodvoc, Anted and Eisu, sometimes thought to mark a divided kingdom with northern and southern halves. The economy rested on sheep and cereal farming in the Cotswolds and on the salt springs of Droitwich. Cassius Dio records that part of the Bodunni, probably the Dobunni, had been subject to the Catuvellauni.
dobunni.e: In 43 part of the Dobunni surrendered to Aulus Plautius, and the region came under Roman control without major recorded conflict. A fort was built at Cirencester, and the town of Corinium Dobunnorum grew into the civitas capital and second largest town of Roman Britain.

duchy-of-the-franks.t: The great Robertian principality between the Seine and the Loire whose dukes overshadowed the last Carolingian kings and became the Capetian dynasty.
duchy-of-the-franks.o: The Robertian family had led the defence of Neustria against the Vikings since Robert the Strong in the 860s, and two of its members, Odo and Robert I, had briefly been kings. In 936 Hugh the Great helped restore the Carolingian Louis IV and was recognised as 'duke of the Franks', second only to the king.
duchy-of-the-franks.r: Hugh the Great held counties and lay abbacies around Paris, Orléans and Tours, including Saint-Martin of Tours and Saint-Denis, giving him more land and men than the king. He controlled royal successions and dealt as an equal with the dukes of Normandy and Burgundy. His son Hugh Capet inherited the title in 956.
duchy-of-the-franks.e: When the last Carolingian king, Louis V, died in 987, the magnates elected Hugh Capet king. The duchy's lands became the royal domain of the new Capetian Kingdom of France, which his descendants ruled for eight centuries.

duchy-of-tuscia.t: Lombard duchy of Tuscany, centred on Lucca, whose duke Desiderius rose to become the last king of the Lombards.
duchy-of-tuscia.o: After the Lombards occupied most of Tuscany in the 570s, the region was organised under dukes, with Lucca as the chief seat. Smaller duchies existed at Chiusi and elsewhere, but Lucca, on the route to Rome later called the Via Francigena, emerged as the dominant centre.
duchy-of-tuscia.r: Little is known of the early dukes. Documents from Lucca, unusually rich for the 8th century, show a society of Lombard landowners, churches and notaries, and Duke Walpert appears in the early 8th century. The Lombard nobleman Desiderius held authority in Tuscia before becoming king in 756. Lucca minted gold coins and was the main town of Lombard Tuscany.
duchy-of-tuscia.e: After Charlemagne's conquest of 774, Tuscia passed to Frankish counts and dukes based at Lucca. By the 9th century these governors were styled margraves, and the region became the March of Tuscany.

dal-riata.t: A Gaelic kingdom spanning north-east Ireland and Argyll whose kings, settling Scotland's west coast, helped make Gaelic the language of medieval Scotland.
dal-riata.o: Dal Riata originated in County Antrim, and by about 500 its rulers held lands across the North Channel in Argyll. Tradition credits Fergus Mor mac Eirc with moving the dynasty to Britain, though the story was shaped by later writers. The Scottish part grew into a federation of kindreds centred on the hillfort of Dunadd.
dal-riata.r: Power was shared among kindreds such as Cenel nGabrain, Cenel Loairn and Cenel nOengusa, recorded in the Senchus fer nAlban, a census of houses and naval levies. Columba's monastery on Iona, founded in 563 with royal favour, made the kingdom a centre of Irish Christianity, scholarship and missionary work reaching Northumbria.
dal-riata.e: Defeat at Mag Rath in 637 cost Dal Riata its Irish lands. In the 8th century it fell under the Picts, and Viking raids from the 790s shattered its sea power. By the mid 9th century its territory and Gaelic culture merged with Pictland into the kingdom later known as Alba, the Kingdom of Scotland.

domain-of-soissons.t: Last Roman-ruled territory in northern Gaul, held by the generals Aegidius and Syagrius until Clovis conquered it in 486.
domain-of-soissons.o: Around 457 the emperor Majorian appointed Aegidius as commander of the Roman army in Gaul. When Majorian was murdered in 461, Aegidius refused to recognise his successors and kept control of the region between the Somme and the Loire, cut off from Italy.
domain-of-soissons.r: Aegidius ruled as a Roman general rather than a king, allying with the Franks and fighting the Visigoths at Orléans in 463. After his death in 464 his son Syagrius held the region from Soissons; Gregory of Tours calls him king of the Romans, though he probably never used the title.
domain-of-soissons.e: In 486 Clovis of the Salian Franks defeated Syagrius near Soissons. Syagrius fled to the Visigothic Kingdom, but Alaric II handed him over, and Clovis had him killed. The domain became the core of the Kingdom of the Franks.

demetae.t: People of south-west Wales whose name survives in Dyfed, and who accepted Roman rule with little recorded fighting.
demetae.o: The Demetae lived in what is now Pembrokeshire and western Carmarthenshire, a region of small defended farmsteads, known as raths, and coastal promontory forts. Ptolemy recorded them in the 2nd century, but no earlier writer describes them, and they were probably a grouping of local communities with long roots in the Iron Age.
demetae.r: Unlike their neighbours the Silures and Ordovices, the Demetae are not recorded as resisting Rome, and their territory needed few garrisons. Farming and cattle-rearing sustained a dispersed population, and the region looked west across the Irish Sea. The Romans mined gold at Dolaucothi on the eastern edge of their land.
demetae.e: After the conquest of Wales in the 70s the Demetae formed a civitas centred on Moridunum, modern Carmarthen, one of the westernmost towns of Roman Britain. The name passed to the post-Roman Kingdom of Dyfed, ruled by a dynasty of Irish descent, and survives in the modern county of Dyfed.

danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.t: The Viking kingdom founded by Guthrum in East Anglia after his defeat by Alfred, the first Danish state in England to accept Christianity.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.o: After Alfred defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878, the Danish leader accepted baptism with the name Aethelstan. In 879 his army settled East Anglia, the former Kingdom of East Anglia, and a treaty with Alfred around 886 fixed the boundary along the Lea, the Ouse and Watling Street.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.r: Guthrum ruled as a Christian king and minted coins under his baptismal name. Danish settlers took land across Norfolk and Suffolk, and soon after his death coins honouring the martyred King Edmund were issued, showing rapid integration. Later rulers, such as Eohric, are poorly documented.
danish-kingdom-of-east-anglia.e: The kingdom joined attacks on English territory, but Edward the Elder conquered it in 917 to 918, and the East Anglian Danes submitted. It became part of the Kingdom of the Anglo-Saxons and later an earldom of England.

duchy-of-franconia.t: The short-lived stem duchy of the Franks in central Germany whose duke Conrad I became king of East Francia in 911.
duchy-of-franconia.o: In the early 10th century the Conradine family won a bloody feud with the Babenbergs for dominance in Franconia, the Frankish heartland along the Main and the middle Rhine. After Adalbert of Babenberg was executed in 906, Conrad the Younger became the leading magnate, recognised as duke of the Franks.
duchy-of-franconia.r: In 911 Conrad was elected king of East Francia as Conrad I, the first non-Carolingian ruler, while his brother Eberhard governed Franconia. Conrad struggled against the Saxon, Bavarian and Swabian dukes and the Magyars. Dying in 918, he reportedly sent the royal insignia to Henry the Fowler of Saxony, his former enemy.
duchy-of-franconia.e: Eberhard accepted Henry I's kingship but rebelled against Otto I and was killed at the Battle of Andernach in 939. Otto did not appoint a new duke; Franconia passed directly to the crown and fragmented into bishoprics such as Würzburg and Bamberg and later secular lordships.

duchy-of-naples.t: Byzantine duchy that became an independent city-state, resisting Lombards and Arabs for nearly five centuries until the Normans took it in 1137.
duchy-of-naples.o: Naples remained in Byzantine hands after the Lombard conquest. In 661 Emperor Constans II appointed Basil as its first duke, subject to the strategos of Sicily. Over the next century the dukes came from local families, and Duke Stephen II, who also became bishop, ruled with little reference to Constantinople.
duchy-of-naples.r: Naples was a Greek-Latin city of merchants and landowners, governed by dukes who also controlled Cumae, Sorrento and Amalfi for a time. Sergius I founded a hereditary dynasty in 840. The duchy fought the Lombards of Benevento, but sometimes allied with Arab raiders, earning papal condemnation. Greek liturgy and learning survived alongside Latin, and Naples kept a strong civic identity.
duchy-of-naples.e: The Normans conquered the surrounding lands in the 11th and 12th centuries. After resisting a siege in 1135–36, Duke Sergius VII submitted to Roger II and was killed in battle in 1137, and Naples joined the Kingdom of Sicily. It later became capital of the Kingdom of Naples.

duchy-of-bavaria.t: One of Germany's oldest territories, a duchy for more than a thousand years under the Agilolfings, Welfs and Wittelsbachs, and the core of modern Bavaria.
duchy-of-bavaria.o: The Bavarians (Baiuvarii) appear in the mid 6th century between the Danube, the Lech and the Alps, a people formed from Germanic groups and the Romanised population. Around 555 the Frankish kings recognised Garibald I of the Agilolfing family as duke. Bavaria later became a stem duchy of East Francia and the Holy Roman Empire.
duchy-of-bavaria.r: The Agilolfing dukes ruled almost as kings, with their own law code, the Lex Baiuvariorum, and bishoprics organised by Saint Boniface in 739 at Salzburg, Regensburg, Freising and Passau. Regensburg was the early capital. From 1180 the Wittelsbach family held the duchy, ruling from Munich, Landshut and Ingolstadt during long periods of division.
duchy-of-bavaria.e: Charlemagne deposed Duke Tassilo III in 788, but the duchy was revived. Albert IV reunited Bavaria in 1505 and imposed primogeniture. In 1623 Maximilian I received the electoral dignity during the Thirty Years' War, and the duchy became the Electorate of Bavaria, later the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806.

dutch-republic.t: The federal republic born of the revolt against Spain, which became the world's leading trading power and a centre of art, science and toleration.
dutch-republic.o: The northern provinces of the Habsburg Netherlands rose against Philip II from 1568 under William the Silent. They allied in the Union of Utrecht in 1579 and renounced Philip by the Act of Abjuration in 1581. After failing to find a new sovereign, the provinces governed themselves as a republic, recognised by Spain in the Peace of Münster in 1648.
dutch-republic.r: Each province was sovereign, sending delegates to the States General at The Hague, while Holland's Grand Pensionary and the Orange-Nassau stadtholders competed for leadership. Founded in 1602, the Dutch East India Company built an Asian trading empire. Amsterdam became Europe's financial centre, and Rembrandt, Vermeer, Spinoza and Huygens worked in relative freedom, though the Reformed church was official.
dutch-republic.e: After the disaster year of 1672, William III led resistance to France and became king of England in 1689. The 18th century brought decline and clashes between Orangists and Patriots. In 1795 French armies and Dutch revolutionaries founded the Batavian Republic.

duchy-of-alamannia.t: The Frankish duchy that ruled the Alemanni of south-west Germany and Switzerland for two centuries, until the Carolingians abolished it at Cannstatt.
duchy-of-alamannia.o: After Clovis' victories over the Alemanni around 496 and 506, the southern Alemanni stayed under Ostrogothic protection until 536, when the Ostrogoth king Witigis ceded them to the Franks. The Merovingian kings then placed the Alemanni under dukes, a region covering modern Baden-Württemberg, Alsace, eastern Switzerland and Bavarian Swabia.
duchy-of-alamannia.r: The dukes governed under Frankish overlordship but often acted independently, especially as Merovingian power weakened. Law was codified in the Pactus and the Lex Alamannorum of the early 8th century. Christianity spread through bishoprics at Constance and Basel and monasteries such as St Gall, founded on the hermitage of Gallus, and Reichenau, founded in 724.
duchy-of-alamannia.e: Duke Lantfrid and his successor Theudebald resisted the rising Carolingian mayors of the palace. In 746 Carloman summoned the Alemannic nobility to Cannstatt and executed many of them, ending the ducal office. Alamannia was then ruled by Frankish counts until the Duchy of Swabia emerged in the early 10th century.

duchy-of-split.t: Short-lived Dalmatian duchy granted to the Bosnian magnate Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić, uniting Split and the central Dalmatian islands under one lord.
duchy-of-split.o: In the struggle for the Hungarian crown between Sigismund of Luxembourg and Ladislaus of Naples, the powerful Bosnian noble Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić backed Ladislaus. In 1403 Ladislaus rewarded him with the title of Duke of Split, together with the islands of Brač, Hvar and Korčula, carving a duchy out of royal Dalmatia.
duchy-of-split.r: Hrvoje ruled from Split while remaining Grand Duke of Bosnia, so the duchy linked the inland Bosnian lands with the Adriatic trade of the city. Split kept its communal statutes and council. Hrvoje's court produced the richly illuminated Glagolitic Missal of Hrvoje, made in Split around 1404, one of the finest Croatian medieval manuscripts.
duchy-of-split.e: Hrvoje later reconciled with Sigismund, but fell from favour and was declared a traitor in 1413; Split threw off his rule and returned to the Hungarian crown. Hrvoje died in 1416, and in 1420 Split passed to Venice, which held it for nearly four centuries.

duchy-of-swabia.t: The stem duchy of south-west Germany, home of the Hohenstaufen emperors, which collapsed with the execution of the last Staufer in 1268.
duchy-of-swabia.o: After the death of the Alemannic dukes in 746, Alamannia was governed by counts. In 915 Count Erchanger defeated King Conrad I's forces at Wahlwies and was proclaimed duke; Conrad executed him in 917, but Burchard II established the duchy, recognised by Henry the Fowler in 919. Swabia covered south-west Germany, Alsace and eastern Switzerland.
duchy-of-swabia.r: Dukes were often royal relatives, and from 1079 the office went to the Staufer family, who became emperors with Conrad III and Frederick Barbarossa. Swabia was rich in monasteries, imperial cities such as Ulm and Augsburg, and lesser nobles. Its knightly culture produced Minnesang poets.
duchy-of-swabia.e: After the fall of the Staufer, the last duke, Conradin, was beheaded at Naples in 1268. The duchy dissolved into many territories, including the County of Württemberg, the Margraviate of Baden, Habsburg lands and free imperial cities, which later formed the Swabian League and the Swabian Circle.

duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.t: North German duchy that briefly passed to Wallenstein during the Thirty Years' War, ruled from a fine Renaissance palace at Güstrow.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.o: Mecklenburg had already been divided before, but the partition of 1621 between the brothers Adolf Frederick I and John Albert II created a lasting Mecklenburg-Güstrow in the east of the country, with Mecklenburg-Schwerin in the west. Rostock and the estates remained shared between the two duchies.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.r: Both dukes were deposed in 1628 by Emperor Ferdinand II, who gave Mecklenburg to his general Albrecht von Wallenstein; Wallenstein governed from Güstrow until Swedish troops restored the dukes in 1631. Government was weakened by powerful noble estates, and the countryside suffered heavily from war and depopulation. The duchy was Lutheran.
duchy-of-mecklenburg-gustrow.e: Gustav Adolph, the last duke, died without male heirs in 1695. A long succession dispute followed until the Treaty of Hamburg in 1701 divided Mecklenburg into the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz.

duchy-of-lucca.t: A small Tuscan duchy created in 1815 for the former queen of Etruria, Maria Luisa of Bourbon, and absorbed by Tuscany in 1847.
duchy-of-lucca.o: The Congress of Vienna gave Lucca to Maria Luisa of Spain, former regent of the Kingdom of Etruria, as compensation for losing Parma, which went to Napoleon's widow Marie Louise. Maria Luisa took possession in 1817 and ruled until her death in 1824.
duchy-of-lucca.r: Maria Luisa revived court life, built roads and the aqueduct of Lucca and encouraged the arts. Her son Charles Louis, Duke Charles I, ruled from 1824, an extravagant and unpredictable prince who spent much time abroad and left government to ministers. The duchy was small, conservative and dependent on Austria.
duchy-of-lucca.e: Under the Vienna settlement, the Bourbons were to return to Parma when Marie Louise died. In October 1847, shortly before her death, Charles Louis handed Lucca to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany and later became Duke of Parma.

dal-fiatach.t: Ruling dynasty of east County Down, centred on Downpatrick, which claimed to be the true Ulaid and held the Ulster kingship until 1177.
dal-fiatach.o: The Dál Fiatach were a dynasty of the Ulaid in what is now east County Down. They claimed descent from the ancient Ulaid royal line, and after the Ulaid were pushed east of the River Bann they became one of the two main powers in the Kingdom of Ulaid, with their stronghold at Dún Lethglaise, Downpatrick, associated with St Patrick's burial.
dal-fiatach.r: Dál Fiatach kings alternated the over-kingship of the Ulaid with the Dal nAraidi. Báetán mac Cairill, who died in 581, is said to have claimed authority as far as the Isle of Man and Scotland. Fiachnae mac Demmáin fought for the kingship in the early 7th century. Their wealth lay in the fertile lands of Lecale and the Ards, and the monasteries of Bangor and Movilla lay nearby.
dal-fiatach.e: From the 11th century their kings were the Mac Duinn Sléibe, MacDunleavy. In 1177 the Anglo-Norman John de Courcy seized Downpatrick and defeated Ruaidrí Mac Duinn Sléibe, founding the Earldom of Ulster and ending Dál Fiatach rule.

duchy-of-brittany.t: The Celtic-speaking peninsula of western France, an independent-minded duchy for six centuries until its heiress Anne married two French kings.
duchy-of-brittany.o: After Viking occupation in the early 10th century, Alan Twisted Beard returned from exile in England and drove the Norse out, completing the reconquest with the victory at Trans in 939. He took the title of duke and made Nantes his base. The duchy's frontier with Anjou and Normandy remained contested for generations.
duchy-of-brittany.r: Brittany kept its own customs, coinage, Estates and courts, with Breton spoken in the west and Gallo and French in the east. The Montfort and Blois families fought the War of the Breton Succession (1341–1364), won by John IV at Auray. Under the Montfort dukes the duchy prospered from salt, linen and shipping and was nearly sovereign.
duchy-of-brittany.e: Francis II's defeat at Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier in 1488 sealed French dominance. His daughter Anne of Brittany married Charles VIII and then Louis XII, and the Edict of Union of 1532 joined the duchy to the Kingdom of France. When the Dauphin, its last duke, became Henry II in 1547, the title merged with the crown.

daunians.t: Iapygian people of northern Apulia, known for their carved stone stelae and painted pottery, who allied with Rome against the Samnites.
daunians.o: The Daunians were the northernmost of the Iapygian peoples of Apulia, settled in the Tavoliere plain and the Gargano from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek legend made the hero Diomedes, returning from Troy, the founder of Arpi and other towns, a story the Daunians themselves seem to have adopted.
daunians.r: Daunian society was organised in large settlements such as Arpi, Canusium, Salapia and Sipontum, with chieftains whose wealth appears in their tombs. Between the 7th and 6th centuries BCE they set up hundreds of anthropomorphic stone stelae near Sipontum, carved with weapons, ornaments and scenes of daily life. Their matt-painted pottery is distinctive. They farmed the plain, raised horses and traded across the Adriatic.
daunians.e: During the Samnite Wars the Daunian towns sided with Rome; Livy records alliances in 318 BCE, and Rome founded Luceria in 314 BCE. Arpi went over to Hannibal after Cannae in 216 BCE and was punished when retaken. The towns became Roman municipia after the Social War, and Daunian identity faded into Roman Apulia.

duchy-of-florence.t: The first Medici duchy, created by Charles V in 1532, under which Cosimo I conquered Siena and turned Florence into a princely state.
duchy-of-florence.o: After the siege of 1529–1530 ended the last Republic of Florence, Emperor Charles V made Alessandro de' Medici hereditary duke in 1532. Alessandro ruled with the support of imperial troops and built the Fortezza da Basso to control the city.
duchy-of-florence.r: Alessandro was murdered by his cousin Lorenzino in 1537, and the 17-year-old Cosimo I de' Medici was chosen to succeed him. Cosimo crushed the republican exiles at Montemurlo that year and built an efficient absolutist state. He founded the Uffizi offices, designed by Giorgio Vasari from 1560, created a navy and the Order of Saint Stephen, and conquered the Republic of Siena in 1555.
duchy-of-florence.e: In 1569 Pope Pius V raised Cosimo to Grand Duke of Tuscany, and the duchy became the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

dyme.t: Westernmost city of Achaea and one of the four cities that refounded the Achaean League in 280 BCE.
dyme.o: Dyme lay on the coastal plain of western Achaea, near Cape Araxos, facing the Ionian Sea. It was one of the twelve cities of Achaea, formed in the early Iron Age from local villages.
dyme.r: Little is known of its government before the Hellenistic age. In 280 BCE Dyme, Patrae, Tritaea and Pharae revived the Achaean League, which grew into a major power. Exposed to the west, Dyme was sacked in 208 BCE by a Roman force during the First Macedonian War, its people enslaved and later ransomed by Philip V of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia.
dyme.e: Dyme passed under Roman control in 146 BCE. In 67 BCE Pompey resettled defeated Cilician pirates there, and it later became a Roman colony under Augustus before declining in favour of Patrae.

duchy-of-neopatras.t: Catalan duchy in southern Thessaly, created on the ruins of the Greek Principality of Thessaly and ruled with Athens by the kings of Sicily and Aragon.
duchy-of-neopatras.o: After the Catalan Company conquered the Duchy of Athens in 1311, it pushed north into Thessaly. When John II Doukas of the Principality of Thessaly died without heirs in 1318, the Catalans occupied the south of the region with its capital Neopatras (modern Ypati) and organised it as a duchy in 1319.
duchy-of-neopatras.r: Neopatras was held together with Athens by the Aragonese kings of Sicily, who appointed vicars-general such as Alfonso Fadrique to govern it. A small Catalan military class ruled over Greeks and Vlachs, following the customs of Barcelona. In 1379-1380 the duchies passed to Peter IV of Aragon, who called the Acropolis the most beautiful jewel in the world.
duchy-of-neopatras.e: Attacks by the Navarrese Company, the Florentine Nerio Acciaioli and the Ottomans broke the Catalan hold. Neopatras fell around 1390, and the Ottomans took Thessaly in the 1390s.

diocese-of-hispania.t: The late Roman administrative unit that grouped the provinces of Iberia and north-west Africa under a single vicar based at Mérida.
diocese-of-hispania.o: The diocese was created in Diocletian's reforms around 297 to 314, grouping the provinces of Baetica, Lusitania, Carthaginiensis, Gallaecia and Tarraconensis with Mauretania Tingitana across the Strait. The Balearica province was added around 369. It formed part of the Praetorian Prefecture of the Gauls.
diocese-of-hispania.r: A vicarius at Emerita Augusta oversaw the provincial governors, mainly in justice and taxation, while separate officers commanded the army. Hispania was largely peaceful in the 4th century, a land of rich villas and cities. Christianity grew strong, as the Council of Elvira shows, and the emperor Theodosius I came from Cauca in the north.
diocese-of-hispania.e: In 409 Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Pyrenees during the usurpation of Constantine III and his general Gerontius. Rome partly restored control with Visigothic help, but the diocese effectively broke up as barbarian kingdoms took over.

duchy-of-sabbioneta.t: The small Lombard duchy of Vespasiano Gonzaga, who built Sabbioneta from scratch as an ideal Renaissance city.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.o: Vespasiano Gonzaga, a soldier and courtier of Philip II of Spain from a cadet branch of the Gonzaga, inherited Sabbioneta and the surrounding lands between Mantua and Parma. From the 1550s he rebuilt the village as a fortified ideal city, and Emperor Rudolf II made it a duchy in 1577.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.r: Sabbioneta was laid out on a regular plan with star-shaped walls, a ducal palace, a long gallery for Vespasiano's art and antiquities, and the Teatro all'Antica by Vincenzo Scamozzi, completed around 1590, one of the first purpose-built theatres in modern Europe. The duke ran a small, tightly controlled court and drew craftsmen and Jewish printers to the town.
duchy-of-sabbioneta.e: Vespasiano died in 1591 without a surviving son, and the duchy passed through his daughter to the Carafa and then other heirs, losing its importance. It was absorbed into Austrian-ruled Lombardy when the Gonzaga lands were seized in 1708.

dal-naraidi.t: Leading kingdom of the Cruthin in south Antrim, whose king Congal Cáech fought for the high kingship and fell at Mag Rath in 637.
dal-naraidi.o: The Dál nAraidi were the leading dynasty of the Cruthin, a people of east Ulster distinguished in early Irish sources from the Ulaid proper. By the 6th century they held south and central County Antrim, with their royal centre in Mag Line near the town of Antrim, and they competed with the Dal Fiatach for the kingship of the Kingdom of Ulaid.
dal-naraidi.r: Fiachnae mac Báetáin, who died in 626, became king of the Ulaid and is said to have campaigned in Britain. Congal Cáech, king of the Ulaid and briefly claimant to the kingship of Tara, allied with Dál Riata but was defeated and killed by Domnall mac Áedo at Mag Rath in 637. St Comgall, founder of the monastery of Bangor, belonged to this people.
dal-naraidi.e: After Mag Rath their power declined, though their kings still held the Ulaid kingship at times until the 10th century. Pressure from Viking raiders, the Uí Néill and the Dal Fiatach reduced them, and by the 12th century their lands passed under Anglo-Norman and Ua Néill rule.

delos.t: The sacred island of Apollo, independent from 314 to 167 BCE, when its sanctuary became a meeting place of kings and a hub of Aegean commerce.
delos.o: Delos, birthplace of Apollo and Artemis in Greek myth, had long been under Athenian control. In 314 BCE, with Antigonus I extending his power into the Aegean, the Athenians were ousted and the Delians governed their island as an independent city, also hosting the Nesiotic League.
delos.r: Independent Delos was run by an archon, council and assembly, while elected hieropoioi managed the sanctuary's lands, loans and treasures; their yearly inscribed accounts are among the richest economic records from antiquity. Kings of Macedon, Egypt and Pergamon built porticoes and dedications. Banking and trade grew, drawing merchants from Italy and the East.
delos.e: In 167 BCE Rome handed Delos to Athens and made it a free port to damage Rhodes; the Delians were expelled to Achaea. Delos then boomed as a slave and grain market until sacked in 88 BCE by the forces of Mithridates VI and again by pirates in 69 BCE. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.t: The marble-quarrying state of the Malaspina and Cybo families on the Tuscan coast, whose white stone supplied Michelangelo and Europe's sculptors.
duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.o: The Malaspina, a feudal family of Lunigiana, ruled Massa, and in 1473 Jacopo Malaspina bought Carrara with its marble quarries. Through the marriage of Ricciarda Malaspina, the state passed to the Cybo family, and Alberico I Cybo-Malaspina was made prince in 1568; it became a duchy in 1664.
duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.r: The rulers governed a narrow strip between the Apuan Alps and the sea. Carrara's marble, quarried since Roman times, was the state's wealth; Michelangelo chose blocks there. Alberico I laid out a new town centre at Massa. The state survived as an imperial fief protected by Spain and its neighbours.
duchy-of-massa-and-carrara.e: The heiress Maria Beatrice Cybo d'Este married Ferdinand of Austria-Este. After Napoleonic rule under Elisa Bonaparte, she was restored in 1814, and on her death in 1829 the duchy passed to her son Francis IV, joining the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

duchy-of-burgundy.t: The wine-rich duchy around Dijon, home of Cluny and Cîteaux, that under its Valois dukes became the seed of a great European power.
duchy-of-burgundy.o: Richard the Justiciar, count of Autun, gathered the counties of western Burgundy and was recognised as duke by around 918. After a century of disputes the duchy went in 1032 to Robert, younger brother of King Henry I, founding a Capetian line that ruled from Dijon for over 300 years.
duchy-of-burgundy.r: The dukes were great vassals of France, governing through their council and the Estates of Burgundy. The duchy was a heartland of monastic reform: Cluny lay on its borders, and Cîteaux, founded in 1098, launched the Cistercian order. Its vineyards in the Côte d'Or were already famous in the Middle Ages.
duchy-of-burgundy.e: When Philip of Rouvres died in 1361, John II of France took the duchy and in 1363 gave it to his son Philip the Bold, founding the Burgundian State. After Charles the Bold fell at Nancy in 1477, Louis XI annexed the duchy to the Kingdom of France.

decapole.t: A league of ten imperial cities of Alsace, founded in 1354 for mutual defence, which survived until Louis XIV absorbed it.
decapole.o: In 1354 Emperor Charles IV joined ten free imperial cities of Alsace in an alliance: Haguenau, Colmar, Wissembourg, Turckheim, Obernai, Kaysersberg, Rosheim, Munster, Sélestat and Mulhouse. They were placed under the imperial bailiff at Haguenau to defend their rights against local lords.
decapole.r: The cities governed themselves but pledged mutual aid, shared costs and met in diets. Mulhouse left in 1515 to ally with the Swiss and Landau joined in 1521. Members were wine and market towns, and some, like Colmar, adopted Lutheranism while others stayed Catholic. The league had no army or capital of its own.
decapole.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 transferred imperial rights in Alsace to France ambiguously, and Louis XIV occupied the cities in 1673. The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1679 confirmed French control, ending the league.

duchy-of-mantua.t: The Gonzaga state of Mantua, whose court commissioned Mantegna, Giulio Romano and Monteverdi before war and plague ruined it.
duchy-of-mantua.o: In 1328 Luigi Gonzaga overthrew the Bonacolsi lords of Mantua and became captain of the people. The Gonzaga ruled as imperial vicars, became marquises in 1433 under Gianfrancesco Gonzaga and dukes in 1530 under Federico II, who also acquired the Duchy of Montferrat.
duchy-of-mantua.r: Mantua's court was among the most brilliant in Italy. Andrea Mantegna painted the Camera degli Sposi for Ludovico III; Isabella d'Este collected art; Giulio Romano built the Palazzo Te for Federico II. Under Vincenzo I, Monteverdi's Orfeo was staged in 1607. The duchy lived from farming, textiles and the condottiere service of its lords.
duchy-of-mantua.e: The main line died out in 1627, and the War of the Mantuan Succession brought an imperial sack in 1630. The Gonzaga-Nevers line ruled until Ferdinando Carlo sided with France and was deposed in 1708, when Austria annexed Mantua.

deisi-muman.t: Kingdom of the Déisi in Waterford and south Tipperary, whose legendary migrations reached Wales and whose name survives in the Decies.
deisi-muman.o: The Déisi were a population group whose name means 'vassals'. The early Irish tale The Expulsion of the Déisi tells how they were driven from Brega near Tara and wandered south, some settling in Munster and others crossing to Dyfed in Wales, where the Kingdom of Dyfed's kings later claimed Déisi descent. In Munster they settled in what is now County Waterford and south Tipperary.
deisi-muman.r: The Déisi Muman were a subject kingdom within the Kingdom of Munster, paying tribute to the Eóganachta of Cashel. The monastery of Lismore, founded by St Mochuda in the 7th century, was one of the great schools of early Ireland and lay in their territory. A northern branch, the Déis Tuaiscirt, later grew into the Dál Cais, the dynasty of Brian Bóruma.
deisi-muman.e: The Ua Fáeláin, O'Phelan, kings ruled the Déisi in the 11th and 12th centuries. After the Anglo-Normans took Waterford in 1170 their lands were granted to settlers, and the kingdom faded around 1200. The name survives in the baronies of Decies in Waterford.

damnonii.t: People of the Clyde valley recorded by Ptolemy, whose territory was crossed by the Antonine Wall and later formed the heart of Strathclyde.
damnonii.o: The Damnonii appear in Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography in the region of the Clyde, Ayrshire and parts of Stirlingshire, with places such as Vanduara and Alauna listed among their settlements. They derived from the Iron Age communities of west central Scotland, who lived in hillforts, crannogs and enclosed farms.
damnonii.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Their land lay on the line of the Antonine Wall, built across the Forth and Clyde isthmus from 142, and was occupied by Roman forts during the periods of Roman advance into Scotland. Their society was otherwise rural and cattle-based, much like their neighbours.
damnonii.e: After the Roman withdrawal to Hadrian's Wall the Damnonii lived beyond the frontier. They are generally regarded as ancestors of the British people of the Clyde, whose Kingdom of Strathclyde was centred on Alt Clut, Dumbarton Rock.

duchy-of-savoy.t: The Alpine duchy of the house of Savoy that straddled France and Italy and grew into the Kingdom of Sardinia, the core of united Italy.
duchy-of-savoy.o: In 1416 Emperor Sigismund raised Count Amadeus VIII of the County of Savoy to the rank of duke. Amadeus later retired and was elected antipope Felix V in 1439. The duchy then included Savoy, Piedmont, Nice, Bresse and the Vaud.
duchy-of-savoy.r: The dukes ruled an Alpine state of pass tolls, farming and soldiers. French occupation from 1536 ended when Emmanuel Philibert recovered his lands at Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559 and moved the capital from Chambéry to Turin in 1563. Savoy lost Geneva and the Vaud but built a centralised military state. Victor Amadeus II gained Sicily in 1713, exchanged for Sardinia in 1720.
duchy-of-savoy.e: From 1720 the dukes were kings of Sardinia. France annexed Savoy in 1792–1815. In 1847 the 'perfect fusion' merged the mainland states with Sardinia, ending the duchy as a separate state; Savoy itself passed to France in 1860.

duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.t: The Este duchy that became the family's main state after the loss of Ferrara, lasting until Italian unification in 1859.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.o: In 1452 Emperor Frederick III made Borso d'Este duke of Modena and Reggio, imperial fiefs held alongside the papal Duchy of Ferrara. When Ferrara passed to the papacy in 1598, Cesare d'Este moved his court to Modena, which became the capital.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.r: The Este rebuilt Modena as a capital, with a ducal palace and the Biblioteca Estense, where the scholar Ludovico Antonio Muratori worked as librarian. The duchy added Mirandola, Correggio and Novellara. After French occupation from 1796, when it joined the Cispadane Republic, the restored duchy passed in 1814 to Francis IV of Austria-Este, who ruled harshly and executed the revolutionary Ciro Menotti in 1831.
duchy-of-modena-and-reggio.e: Francis V fled after the Austrian defeat in 1859. The duchy joined the United Provinces of Central Italy and was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

domnonee.t: Breton kingdom of northern Brittany, named after Dumnonia in Britain, whose king Judicael treated with Dagobert I as an equal.
domnonee.o: Migrants from Dumnonia in south-west Britain, the land of modern Devon and Cornwall, settled the northern coast of Armorica in the 5th and 6th centuries and gave it the name of their homeland. Its early rulers are known mainly from saints' lives, which may preserve legend.
domnonee.r: The kingdom stretched along the Channel coast from the Rance to the Morlaix area. Its life centred on monastic foundations such as Saint-Malo, Dol and Saint-Pol-de-Léon, linked to saints from Wales and Cornwall. The chronicle of Fredegar records that King Judicael met Dagobert I at Clichy in 636 and made peace with the Franks.
domnonee.e: In the 9th century Domnonée was absorbed into the Kingdom of Brittany created by Nominoe and Erispoe. The bishopric of Dol and the later counties of Penthièvre and Léon preserved parts of its territory.

duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.t: The Norman duchy of Robert Guiscard, which drove the Byzantines out of southern Italy and laid the groundwork for the Kingdom of Sicily.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.o: Norman mercenaries in Byzantine Apulia elected William Iron Arm as their count at Melfi around 1042–1043. His half-brother Robert Guiscard took over, and in 1059 Pope Nicholas II invested him at Melfi as duke of Apulia, Calabria and, in prospect, Sicily, making the papacy the duchy's overlord.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.r: Guiscard captured Bari in 1071, ending Byzantine rule in Italy, and Salerno in 1077, which became his capital. The duchy ruled Greek-speaking Calabria and Lombard and Latin Apulia, keeping Byzantine officials and Greek monasteries alongside Latin bishops. Its army also invaded the Byzantine Empire across the Adriatic in 1081, and in 1084 sacked Rome while rescuing Pope Gregory VII.
duchy-of-apulia-and-calabria.e: After Guiscard's death in 1085, his son Roger Borsa and grandson William II struggled to control rebellious barons. When William died childless in 1127, his cousin Roger II of the County of Sicily claimed the duchy, and in 1130 merged it into the new Kingdom of Sicily.

duchy-of-lorraine.t: The duchy between France and the Empire, ruled for seven centuries by one dynasty from Nancy before passing to France in 1766.
duchy-of-lorraine.o: Lorraine grew from the Duchy of Upper Lorraine, created in 959 when the Duchy of Lotharingia was divided. In 1048 Emperor Henry III gave it to Gerard of Alsace, whose descendants ruled until 1737. The dukes settled on Nancy as their capital and held their lands as vassals of the Holy Roman Empire.
duchy-of-lorraine.r: The duchy was bilingual, French in the west and German in the east, and surrounded by the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun. René II defeated and killed Charles the Bold before Nancy in 1477. The Guise branch led the Catholic League in France, and Nancy's Renaissance and baroque palaces reflected a brilliant court.
duchy-of-lorraine.e: France occupied Lorraine repeatedly in the 17th century; Duke Leopold recovered it in 1697. In 1737 Francis Stephen exchanged it for Tuscany, and the deposed Polish king Stanisław Leszczyński ruled it for life. On his death in 1766 it was annexed to the Kingdom of France.

duchy-of-brabant.t: The duchy of Brussels, Leuven and Antwerp, famous for its charter of liberties, the Joyous Entry, and the economic heart of the Low Countries.
duchy-of-brabant.o: The counts of Louvain had held the title of duke of Lower Lorraine since 1106. Around 1183 Henry I began styling himself duke of Brabant, and after the Diet of Schwäbisch Hall in 1190 the County of Louvain and its neighbouring lands formed the Duchy of Brabant.
duchy-of-brabant.r: Brabant's dukes ruled with powerful towns: Brussels, Leuven, Antwerp and 's-Hertogenbosch. John I won Limburg at Worringen in 1288. The Joyous Entry of 1356 bound Duchess Joanna to respect the estates' rights, a charter sworn by every later ruler. Cloth, then Antwerp's world trade in the 16th century, made Brabant the richest part of the Low Countries.
duchy-of-brabant.e: Brabant passed to Philip the Good in 1430 and joined the Burgundian State, then the Habsburg Netherlands. The Dutch Revolt split it: the north went to the Dutch Republic in 1648, the south stayed in the Spanish Netherlands and Austrian Netherlands, rose in the Brabant Revolution of 1789, and was annexed by France in 1795.

duchy-of-rome.t: Byzantine district around Rome in which the popes gradually took over government, the seed of the Papal States.
duchy-of-rome.o: After the Lombard invasion, the territory around Rome remained in Byzantine hands, cut off from Ravenna by Lombard Spoleto. A duke (dux) commanded its garrison under the exarch of Ravenna. From the pontificate of Gregory the Great (590–604), who organised Rome's food supply and defence, the popes became the area's real leaders.
duchy-of-rome.r: The duke led the local militia while the pope administered the vast Church estates, fed the city and negotiated with the Lombards. A local military aristocracy grew powerful. Disputes with Constantinople over doctrine and taxation, especially Iconoclasm under Leo III, loosened ties to the empire. King Liutprand's gift of Sutri to the pope in 728 was its first territorial grant.
duchy-of-rome.e: When the Lombards took Ravenna in 751 and threatened Rome, Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps and gained the protection of Pepin the Short in 754. Pepin's donation of 756 created the Papal States, into which the duchy was absorbed.

duchy-of-bohemia.t: The Czech duchy of the Přemyslid dynasty, home of Saint Wenceslas, which grew from Prague into a strong state and a kingdom of the Empire.
duchy-of-bohemia.o: Bořivoj I, the first historically attested Přemyslid, was baptised around 870, probably by Methodius, while under Great Moravian overlordship. After Great Moravia fell, the Přemyslids of Prague unified the Bohemian tribes. In 895 they sought East Frankish protection, and Bohemia became tied to the German kingdom.
duchy-of-bohemia.r: Dukes ruled from Prague Castle through a network of castle districts. Wenceslas, murdered by his brother Boleslaus I in 935, became the country's patron saint. Boleslaus II founded the bishopric of Prague in 973. Dukes were vassals of the German kings, while slave trade, silver and later colonisation shaped the economy.
duchy-of-bohemia.e: Vratislaus II received a personal royal title in 1085 and Vladislaus II in 1158. In 1198 Ottokar I secured a hereditary royal crown, confirmed by the Golden Bull of Sicily in 1212, and the duchy became the Kingdom of Bohemia, a leading state of the Empire.

duchy-of-trent.t: Lombard frontier duchy in the Adige valley guarding the Brenner route into Italy against Franks and Bavarians.
duchy-of-trent.o: Soon after the Lombard invasion of 568, a duchy was set up at Tridentum (Trento) to control the Adige valley, the main route from the Brenner Pass into the Po plain. Paul the Deacon names Euin as its first duke, who repelled Frankish invasions in the 570s and 580s and married a Bavarian princess.
duchy-of-trent.r: The dukes of Trent were military lords on a sensitive frontier, dealing by war and marriage with the Franks and the Bavarians to the north. Their territory covered much of modern Trentino and the upper Adige. Duke Alahis rebelled against King Cunipert, seized Pavia and was killed at the battle of Coronate around 689. Otherwise little is recorded of their government.
duchy-of-trent.e: After Charlemagne's conquest of the Lombard Kingdom in 774, Trent was placed under Frankish counts as part of the Carolingian Kingdom of Italy. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II gave the county to the bishops of Trent, founding the prince-bishopric.

duchy-of-limburg.t: A small duchy in the hills east of the Meuse whose succession war ended at the battle of Worringen in 1288, binding it to Brabant for five centuries.
duchy-of-limburg.o: The castle of Limbourg on the Vesdre was built in the early 11th century, and around 1065 Walram Udo of the house of Arlon became count of Limburg. His son Henry I claimed the duchy of Lower Lorraine, and later rulers kept the ducal title for their own lands.
duchy-of-limburg.r: Limburg was a land of pasture, woods and later cloth and lead mining around Verviers and the Vesdre valley. Its dukes, among them Waleran III, intermarried with Luxembourg and the Rhineland nobility. When the line ended in 1283, John I of Brabant fought for the inheritance and won at Worringen in 1288.
duchy-of-limburg.e: Limburg was then ruled with the Duchy of Brabant, passing to the Burgundian State, the Habsburg Netherlands and the Spanish Netherlands. In 1661 the Overmaas lands were divided with the Dutch Republic. France annexed the rest in 1795.

duchy-of-spoleto.t: Powerful Lombard duchy of central Italy whose later dukes, Guy and Lambert, became kings of Italy and emperors in the 9th century.
duchy-of-spoleto.o: Lombard warriors under Faroald I took Spoleto in the Umbrian Apennines around 570, cutting the Byzantine route between Rome and Ravenna. The duchy grew into a large territory covering much of Umbria, the Marche and Abruzzo, largely independent of the kings in Pavia.
duchy-of-spoleto.r: The dukes of Spoleto acted like rulers in their own right, waging war on the Byzantines and sometimes defying the Lombard kings; Transamund II was deposed by Liutprand. After 774 it passed to Frankish dukes but kept its weight. Guy of Spoleto was crowned King of Italy in 889 and emperor in 891, and his son Lambert also became emperor. The town's Romanesque churches reflect its medieval wealth.
duchy-of-spoleto.e: In the 10th to 12th centuries the duchy was often held with Camerino or Tuscany by imperial appointees. Frederick Barbarossa sacked Spoleto in 1155. In 1198 Pope Innocent III took the duchy into the Papal States, where it remained until 1860.

duchy-of-milan.t: Northern Italy's richest state under the Visconti and Sforza, scene of Leonardo's Last Supper, and later a prize held by Spain and Austria.
duchy-of-milan.o: In 1395 Gian Galeazzo Visconti bought the title of duke from Emperor Wenceslas, turning the Lordship of Milan into an imperial duchy. Gian Galeazzo expanded it far into central Italy before his sudden death in 1402.
duchy-of-milan.r: After the last Visconti, Filippo Maria, died in 1447 and the Golden Ambrosian Republic failed, the condottiere Francesco Sforza became duke in 1450. Milan was a centre of arms making, silk and wool, with a strong bureaucracy. Ludovico Sforza employed Leonardo da Vinci, who painted the Last Supper. France invaded in 1499; after the last Sforza died in 1535 Habsburg Spain ruled through governors, followed by Austria from 1714, whose reforms suited thinkers such as Cesare Beccaria.
duchy-of-milan.e: Napoleon's army entered Milan in 1796, and the duchy was replaced by the Transpadane Republic and then in 1797 the Cisalpine Republic. Austria later ruled Lombardy as part of the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia.

deciates.t: Ligurian people near Antibes whose attacks on Greek colonies brought the first Roman army into southern Gaul in 154 BCE.
deciates.o: The Deciates were a Ligurian people living in the hills behind Antipolis (Antibes), a colony of Massalia. Polybius is the main source.
deciates.r: Like other Ligurian peoples of the coast they lived in fortified hilltop settlements and combined farming and herding with raids on the Greek coastal towns.
deciates.e: In 154 BCE the Deciates and the Oxybii besieged Antipolis and Nikaia, and Massalia appealed to the Roman Republic. The consul Quintus Opimius defeated them and handed part of their land to Massalia. Their territory later became part of the province of Alpes Maritimae.

duchy-of-bar.t: A Lorraine county raised to a duchy, divided between French and imperial allegiance, and united with the Duchy of Lorraine under René of Anjou's heirs.
duchy-of-bar.o: Bar-le-Duc's castle was built in the 10th century by Duke Frederick of Upper Lorraine. Around 1033 his heiress Sophie of Bar married Louis of Mousson, count of Montbéliard, and their descendants ruled the county of Bar as a separate principality between Champagne and Lorraine.
duchy-of-bar.r: The counts ruled a fertile land along the Meuse and Ornain. After a defeat by Philip IV, the Treaty of Bruges in 1301 made the western part, the Barrois mouvant, a fief of the French crown, while the rest stayed imperial. Robert I became the first duke in 1354. René of Anjou inherited Bar in 1430 after marrying Isabella of Lorraine.
duchy-of-bar.e: René's grandson René II united Bar and the Duchy of Lorraine in 1480, and the two shared rulers thereafter. Like Lorraine, Bar passed to Stanisław Leszczyński in 1737 and was annexed to the Kingdom of France on his death in 1766.

duchy-of-bourbon.t: The central French duchy of a Capetian branch whose last great duke betrayed Francis I and whose cousins later became kings of France.
duchy-of-bourbon.o: The lords of Bourbon had held the Bourbonnais since the 10th century. In 1272 the heiress Beatrice of Bourbon married Robert of Clermont, son of Louis IX, and in 1327 Charles IV raised the barony to a duchy for their son Louis I, creating the Capetian house of Bourbon.
duchy-of-bourbon.r: The dukes ruled from Moulins and gathered Forez, Beaujolais, Auvergne and La Marche through marriage and inheritance, making their lands one of France's largest princely blocs. Louis II, called the Good Duke, was a model crusading prince. Anne of France and her husband Peter II governed the kingdom during the minority of Charles VIII.
duchy-of-bourbon.e: Charles III, constable of France, fell out with Francis I, who claimed his lands; he joined Charles V in 1523 and was killed leading the sack of Rome in 1527. His lands were confiscated and joined to the Kingdom of France, but a younger Bourbon line gave France Henry IV.

duchy-of-benevento.t: Southern Lombard duchy and later principality that outlived the Lombard Kingdom by three centuries, a centre of southern Italian culture.
duchy-of-benevento.o: Lombard warriors under Zotto established themselves at Beneventum in Campania around 571, perhaps first as soldiers in Byzantine pay. Under Arechis I the duchy expanded across most of southern Italy, apart from the Byzantine coastal cities, Calabria and Apulia's heel.
duchy-of-benevento.r: Benevento was effectively independent of Pavia; Duke Grimoald I even became King of the Lombards in 662. When Charlemagne took the north in 774, Arechis II took the title of prince and claimed the Lombard heritage, building the church of Santa Sofia. The duchy developed the Beneventan script and was a cultural centre linked to Monte Cassino. Civil war in 849 split it into Benevento and Salerno, and Capua later broke away.
duchy-of-benevento.e: Weakened by Arab raids, Byzantines and Normans, the principality shrank. In 1051 the city placed itself under Pope Leo IX, and when the last prince, Landulf VI, died in 1077, Benevento became a papal enclave, while its lands passed to the Normans.

deceangli.t: People of north-east Wales, the first target of Roman campaigns into Wales in 48, whose lead mines soon stamped their name on Roman ingots.
deceangli.o: The Deceangli lived in what is now Flintshire and Denbighshire, between the Dee estuary and the Clwyd valley, a region of hillforts such as Moel Hiraddug and Penycloddiau. They were probably a small Iron Age grouping of local communities and are first named by Tacitus.
deceangli.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society beyond the archaeology of their hillforts and farms. Their territory was rich in lead and silver ores on Halkyn Mountain, which the Romans quickly exploited; lead pigs found near Chester carry the inscription DECEANGL and a date of 74, showing that mining was organised under the name of the people.
deceangli.e: In 48 the governor Ostorius Scapula marched against the Deceangli, ravaging their land almost to the Irish Sea before trouble among the Brigantes recalled him. The area was secured by the fortress of Chester in the 70s, and the Deceangli are not known to have formed a civitas of Roman Britain.
